_comment: Writes demo/demo_timeline_demo.json: the full product demo (about 4.5 minutes, no slides), Video.mp4 in Group19.zip. Generated by demo/make_timeline_demo.py; record with REPLAY_STEP_PACE=0.35.

steps.say: ThreadPilot, the general manager’s co-pilot. One working day at a knitwear factory, on its own records: 1 April 2026.
07:00 · Before she asks anything, the day is on one screen: RED, 8 orders overdue, assembly below normal for 6 days, 3 decisions.
Each decision has one button. “Review options” runs the queue simulation for ORD-029, which will miss 1 April.
Moving ORD-029 up saves it 5 days but makes 6 other orders 11 days later in total, so it recommends keeping the current order.
Drafted before she asks: the two stalled orders already have a chase-up, written from the records, not by the model.
“Review & send” opens the preview: to washing, 9 days idle, 3 days overdue. She reads it and confirms.
Sent and logged; ORD-002 leaves the list. Nothing went out before her click.
Every chart has an “i”: what it shows, how to read it, and why it is computed that way.
“Normal” is the previous 8 same weekdays (Sundays are closed): measured on this factory, it cut false alerts from 0.67 to 0.1 a month.
The 07:00 briefing is written on a schedule: yesterday, what is at risk, what to decide, each point with its records.
09:40 · On the floor, she asks in her own words. “Did anything go wrong yesterday?”
A discovery tool ranks 34 findings by tier and score, so five make the page and the rest wait: the assembly drop first.
A judgement tool with a written definition: 455 pieces against 687–807 for the previous eight Tuesdays, 39% below.

type.text: How is the TrendCart order doing?

steps.say: A vague question: TrendCart has six active orders, so it asks instead of guessing.
Only one is a scarf: ORD-005, at knitting, due 20 April.
“Show more”: the planner’s reading, each tool with its arguments, and the exact rows the answer came from.
A second order in the same chat: ORD-120, 1,500 vests at assembly, due 17 March.
It remembers the chat: “the scarf one” is ORD-005, back from two answers ago. Not late yet, but the queue projects it 6 working days late, and it says why.

type.text: What was the factory’s total output yesterday?

steps.say: A total that must not exist: the four stages are steps on the same pieces, so it lists them and refuses to add them up.
11:15 · A customer wants 800 hoodies by the 25th.

type.text: Can we take 800 hoodies by the 25th?

steps.say: It asks the one thing that changes the answer: ready at the factory, or delivered?
An estimate, not a yes: the queue’s finish date, the on-time chance, the bottleneck, outside workshops that could take it.
The Feasibility page runs the same tool over the whole queue.
Our own queue finishes 30 April, after the 25th; an eligible outside workshop could make it in time.
Why: queued work plus this order is over capacity at the later stages before the 25th.
14:30 · The core task: chase a stalled order, typed the way it is said on the floor.

type.text: ORD 5 hasn’t moved in a week, chase knitting

steps.say: It checks the claim against the record first (last activity 24 March, 8 days: true), then drafts to knitting.
Preview first. Nothing is sent until the manager confirms this exact draft.
Sent from the manager’s own mailbox.

type.text: Remind me tmrw 10am if knitting doesn’t reply

steps.say: A standing watch, not a note: at 10:00 tomorrow the server checks, and notifies only if no reply was recorded.
Every action is logged: the Activity Log shows both chase-ups with recipient, orders and subject.
It also speaks first, but rationed: an alert email only for a decision needed today, at most 3 a day, never the same item twice in 24 hours.
Honesty under pressure. A question the data cannot answer:

type.text: What revenue did the TrendCart orders bring in this quarter?

steps.say: No prices in the records, so no revenue figure. It says what it can answer instead.

type.text: Chase ord 29, stuck at washing since last wk

steps.say: A wrong premise: the record says ORD-029 moved today. It says so, and asks before writing anything.
No order ID, only a description: three orders match, so it lists them instead of picking one.
“The vest one” narrows that list to ORD-120 and drafts to assembly. Still nothing sent.
Not in the records, and it says so. It never invents an order, a stage or a number.
Every number comes from a tool with its rows · it asks instead of guessing · it says what the data cannot answer · nothing leaves without a confirmed preview.
